query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, diffusion-bonded aluminide coating applied to the as‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will form a protective Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure that significantly improves its oxygen resistance without degrading its characteristic mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin aluminide coating (via pack cementation or a similar surface modification method) that provides an aluminum reservoir on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure in an oxygen-containing atmosphere (air) at approximately 1000 °C for up to 100 hours under static or cyclic mechanical loading similar to the baseline conditions (strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1 for high-temperature tests and standard load for room-temperature tensile tests).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 film on the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: The aluminide layer reacts with environmental oxygen at elevated temperatures to form a stable, slow-growing Al2O3 scale, which protects the underlying alloy from further oxidation while leaving the bulk microstructure—and thus the mechanical properties—largely unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminide-coated alloy will show a markedly reduced weight gain and oxide scale thickness during high-temperature exposure compared to the uncoated alloy, while maintaining tensile ductility and yield strength similar to cast HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.baseline: Uncoated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits poor oxygen resistance despite its useful ductility and yield strength.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to single, surface-based interventions applied as thin coatings. Effects outside the tested temperature (around 1000 °C), atmosphere (air), exposure duration (~100 hours), and mechanical-loading conditions remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how the coating will perform under thermal cycling or mechanical deformation beyond the tested static conditions, and long-term adhesion under service conditions needs validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of specimens: one group of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr remains uncoated (control), and the other group receives the aluminide coating. Subject both groups to air exposure at 1000 °C for 100 hours under the same controlled mechanical-loading conditions. After exposure, conduct surface oxidation assessments, weight gain measurements, SEM/EDS analysis for oxide scale integrity, and mechanical tests (room temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength tests).
measurements: Weight gain measurements to assess oxidation rate
Surface and cross-sectional SEM/EDS for oxide scale morphology and thickness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminide-coated specimens exhibit oxidation characteristics (e.g., weight gain or scale spallation) comparable to or worse than the uncoated specimens, or if their mechanical performance deviates significantly (e.g., more than a 15% reduction in ductility or yield strength) from the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
